summary: Describes an architecture for SNMP management frameworks, designed to be modular so the SNMP standards can evolve. It replaces RFC 2261 and was itself replaced by RFC 2571.

eli5.summary: It is the blueprint of the SNMP management system, updated from an earlier draft and later replaced again.

questions: how does snmp access control work
subtitle: A modular blueprint for building SNMP management systems that can evolve over time.

tldr.problem: SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) needs a flexible architecture that can support security, authentication and diverse network management features while remaining simple and allowing for future improvements without breaking existing systems.
tldr.mechanism: The architecture defines an SNMP engine with pluggable subsystems: a message processing subsystem (handling protocol versions), a security subsystem (authentication and encryption), and an access control subsystem (authorization). These are orchestrated by a dispatcher that routes operations to the appropriate application (a manager or agent).
tldr.outcome: SNMP implementations can be modular and extensible, allowing security, message handling and access control to evolve independently. It was replaced by RFC 2571, which added clarifications. This is the architectural foundation for SNMPv3.

facts.label: Major subsystems
facts.value: 5 (message processor, security, access control, dispatcher, applications)

today: RFC 2271 was obsoleted by RFC 2571, which is the current SNMP architecture standard. This document laid the foundation for SNMPv3 and remains the architectural blueprint for modern SNMP implementations, which support multiple security models and message processing versions.

sections.title: Introduction and Goals
sections.content:
This document defines a vocabulary and architecture for describing SNMP management frameworks. It is designed to be modular, allowing different parts of the SNMP specification to evolve at different rates. SNMP management systems consist of network managers (command generators) that monitor and control managed elements (like routers), agents on those elements that respond to queries, and a shared SNMP message protocol.

The architecture was driven by several goals: reusing existing work from SNMPv2u and SNMPv2*; addressing the critical need for secure SET (configuration) support, the most important deficiency in SNMPv1 and SNMPv2c; allowing parts of the standard to move forward even without consensus on all pieces; supporting multiple security models and protocol versions; keeping SNMP as simple as possible; and making it inexpensive to deploy minimal implementations while still supporting features needed in large networks.
sections.eli5: SNMP is complicated, so this document breaks it into building blocks. Each block has a clear job (like checking security or handling messages) so people can design and improve them separately without breaking everything else.

sections.title: Core Architecture Components
sections.content:
The architecture centers on an SNMP engine identified by a unique engine ID. The engine contains several subsystems. The Message Processing Subsystem handles different SNMP protocol versions (like SNMPv1, SNMPv2c, and SNMPv3), decoding incoming messages and encoding outgoing ones. The Security Subsystem validates sender identity, optionally decrypts messages, and enforces the security level (authentication and encryption options). The Access Control Subsystem determines whether a user is authorized to access specific management information.

A Dispatcher routes incoming messages to the appropriate subsystem and application, and routes outgoing messages from applications through the subsystems. SNMP applications may be managers (command generators that query devices) or agents (command responders that serve data). Some entities act as both manager and agent, or as proxy agents that forward requests.

The architecture defines contexts, which partition management information. A context is identified by an engine ID (the SNMP engine being queried) and a context name (a label within that engine). This allows a single SNMP agent to serve multiple independent management information bases.
sections.eli5: An SNMP system is like a building with different departments. The message processor is the front desk (greeting visitors in different languages). Security is the guard who checks that visitors are who they say they are. Access control is the receptionist who checks if you're allowed on this floor. The dispatcher sends you to the right office. Managers are office workers asking questions, and agents are assistants answering them.

sections.title: Identity and Naming
sections.content:
The architecture introduces several key naming concepts. A Principal is the authenticated sender of a message (a user or application). A securityName is the name of a principal within a security model (e.g., a username). A Model-dependent security ID is the internal identifier used by a specific security implementation (e.g., a hash or encrypted token).

Management information is organized around contexts. An snmpEngineID uniquely identifies an SNMP engine (using an algorithm to ensure uniqueness across administrative domains). A contextName is a label that identifies a specific context within that engine (for example, 'public' or 'private'). Together, these form a scopedPDU, a Protocol Data Unit that includes the context and the actual management request or response.

Other architectural elements include securityLevel, which specifies whether authentication and encryption are required; maxSizeResponseScopedPDU, the maximum size for a response; and a Local Configuration Datastore where each SNMP engine stores configuration about security users, access control lists, and engine parameters.
sections.eli5: Every message says who's sending it, which SNMP engine it's for, and which context (like a folder) it's about. The engine also keeps a local file of settings about users, permissions, and secrets.

sections.title: Subsystem Interfaces
sections.content:
The architecture defines abstract interfaces between the dispatcher and each subsystem, allowing modular implementations. The Dispatcher Primitives include operations to generate outgoing requests or notifications, process incoming requests or notifications, generate outgoing responses, and process incoming responses. A primitive for registering responsibility ensures each subsystem knows which PDU types it handles.

The Message Processing Subsystem Primitives include preparing outgoing SNMP requests or notifications (encoding them for the network), preparing outgoing responses (encoding responses), and extracting data elements from incoming SNMP messages (decoding them). These primitives are version-specific (SNMPv1, SNMPv2c, SNMPv3 each has different encoding).

The Security Subsystem Primitives include generating request or notification messages (applying authentication and encryption), processing incoming messages (validating authentication and decrypting), and generating response messages. The Access Control Subsystem Primitives check whether a principal has permission to access specific management information.

Common Primitives include releasing state reference information when transactions complete, and scenario diagrams illustrate how a manager or agent uses these primitives to send and receive SNMP messages.
sections.eli5: The architecture defines a standard 'contract' between components. The dispatcher says to a security module, 'Authenticate this message and encrypt it,' and the security module knows what to do. This lets people design the security module independently from the dispatcher.

sections.title: Framework Modular Design
sections.content:
The architecture supports multiple implementations of each subsystem. For example, implementations may support multiple Message Processing Models (SNMPv1, SNMPv2c for community-based access control, SNMPv3 for user-based security). Similarly, multiple Security Models may be available, such as a simple community-based model (no real authentication) or a user-based model with strong authentication and encryption.

Access Control Models may also vary. A simple model might grant access based on IP address; a sophisticated model might use detailed role-based access control.

The modular design means that a manager might support SNMPv1, SNMPv2c and SNMPv3, allowing it to interoperate with agents using different versions. An agent might offer only SNMPv3 for security. New message processing models, security protocols (like stronger encryption algorithms) and access control schemes can be added without changing the core architecture.

Additionally, the architecture defines objects in the SNMP Management Information Base (MIB) that allow remote management of engine configuration (like user definitions and security settings), subject to local policy and access control rules.
sections.eli5: The system is like using pluggable modules. You can plug in a security module that uses passwords, or one that uses certificates. You can use SNMPv1 (simple, old) or SNMPv3 (modern, secure). Managers and agents can support whichever modules they need.
